summary: Defines two Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) extended key usage values and a public key certificate extension that carries wireless LAN network names (SSIDs). This lets a certificate say it is meant for authentication in PPP and WLAN settings. It is a standards-track document that obsoletes RFC 3770.

eli5.summary: A certificate is like an ID badge. This adds labels to the badge saying which kinds of doors it may open, including which Wi-Fi network names it is meant for.

subtitle: Certificate markers that tell a Wi-Fi or dial-up client which of its certificates fits which network.

tldr.problem: A device that holds several X.509 certificates has to pick the right one when it joins a PPP link or a wireless LAN, and without hints it needs the user to choose.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two extended key usage values (EAP over PPP and EAP over LAN) and a certificate extension that lists up to 32-octet network names (SSIDs), so software can pick a certificate automatically.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track document that replaces RFC 3770 with small corrections, and it warns that SSIDs are not unique and are visible to eavesdroppers.

today: RFC 4334 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced RFC 3770.

sections.title: Why Certificates Need Labels
sections.content:
Several EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) methods use X.509 public key certificates. EAP-TLS, for example, can run over PPP, which is used for dial-up and VPN, or over IEEE 802.1X, which provides port-based network access control for Ethernet, Token Ring, wireless LANs and other IEEE 802 networks.

Picking the right client certificate automatically is highly desirable. Certificate extensions that name the intended environment reduce the need for user input and help separate the administration of certificates used in different environments.

The same wireless station might authenticate to a corporate WLAN and a public hotspot. If the two operators have no roaming agreement, the 802.1X supplicant has to choose a certificate for the network it is on, and a list of network names in the certificate makes that choice automatic.
sections.eli5: If you carry a keyring with many badges, you do not want to guess which one opens each door. Labels on the badges let you pick the right one quickly.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3770
sections.content:
This document is primarily the same as RFC 3770, which it obsoletes. It lists six significant changes:

  • The normative ASN.1 reference now matches RFC 3280, so both documents have the same dependencies.
  • The critical-bit discussion is aligned with RFC 3280, and the key usage discussion is expanded.
  • A typographical error in the object identifier of the WLAN SSID attribute certificate attribute is corrected.
  • The SSID extension may appear in certificates that have no extended key usage extension.
  • The terms peer, EAP Server and supplicant replace client and server.
  • The object identifier of the extended key usage extension is no longer repeated, because RFC 3280 lists it.
sections.eli5: This is a cleaned-up second edition. It fixes a typo in a number and uses the same names for things as the other rulebooks.

sections.title: EAP Extended Key Usage Values
sections.content:
RFC 3280 defines the extended key usage certificate extension, which lists the purposes the certified public key may be used for. This RFC adds two KeyPurposeId values: id-kp-eapOverPPP (id-kp 13) and id-kp-eapOverLAN (id-kp 14).

The first says the key suits a peer using EAP in the PPP environment. The second says it suits a peer using EAP in the LAN environment. Including both says the key suits either one.

The extension MAY be critical or non-critical, at the issuer's option. Applications MAY require it, and MAY require a particular value in it. If several values are present, the application need not recognise all of them as long as the one it needs is there.

If a certificate has both a key usage extension and an extended key usage extension, both MUST be processed independently. The certificate MUST only be used for a purpose consistent with both, and if no purpose is consistent with both it MUST NOT be used for any purpose.
sections.eli5: Two stickers are defined: one says good for dial-up, the other says good for the local network. A badge can carry either or both, and you only need to find the sticker you care about.

sections.title: The WLAN SSID Extension and Attribute
sections.content:
The WLAN SSID certificate extension holds a list of Service Set Identifiers, the network names of IEEE 802.11 WLANs. It is always non-critical, and the list MAY be used to select the right certificate for a particular WLAN. It is identified by id-pe-wlanSSID (id-pe 13).

Its syntax is SSIDList ::= SEQUENCE SIZE (1..MAX) OF SSID, where SSID ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE (1..32)). If the same certificate also carries an extended key usage extension, that extension MUST include id-kp-eapOverLAN.

When the public key certificate has no SSID extension, an attribute certificate can associate a list of SSIDs with it instead. The WLAN SSID attribute certificate attribute is identified by id-aca-wlanSSID (id-aca 7) and uses exactly the same SSIDList syntax.
sections.eli5: The badge can also list the names of the Wi-Fi networks it is meant for. If the badge cannot hold the list, a separate note stapled to it can.

sections.title: Handling Duplicate Network Names
sections.content:
SSID values are unmanaged, so the same SSID can appear in certificates meant for different WLANs. When that happens, automatic selection fails and the implementation SHOULD ask the user to choose the correct certificate.

If no user is available, each candidate certificate MAY be tried until one succeeds. To reduce user involvement, an implementation can keep a cache of Access Point MAC addresses, or of the EAP server identity, with which a certificate has already authenticated successfully. The RFC notes that RADIUS is usually the authentication service in WLAN deployments.
sections.eli5: If two badges both say Coffee Shop, you may have to ask which one is right, or try them one after another. Remembering which one worked last time saves effort.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The certification authority MUST make sure the correct extended key usage and SSID values are put into each certificate. A wrong value could make a relying party reject a good certificate or accept one that ought to be rejected.

A certificate that lists several SSIDs reveals information about several WLANs, not only the one being accessed. In most situations, including EAP-TLS, the peer can validate the EAP server's certificate before sending its own, which helps it decide whether to present the certificate. The list of SSIDs is also visible to eavesdroppers on the WLAN, so where that is a concern, different peer certificates ought to be used for each WLAN.

Trying every certificate in turn discloses each one's SSID list, so that approach is RECOMMENDED only when user selection is unavailable or impractical. The RFC argues that SSID disclosure is of little concern in practice, because other WLAN management messages include the SSID even when the beacon masks it.
sections.eli5: Anyone nearby can read the network names on your badge, so if that bothers you, use a different badge for each network.
